title: Transport in magnetic-topological-insulator nanoribbons containing multiple superconductor-proximitized sectors
authors: Javier Osca, Sungguen Ryu, Rosa López, Llorenç Serra
abstract: Transport in devices with multiple proximitized sectors depends heavily on the complex phases of the pairing gaps of those sectors. We investigate magnetic topological insulator nanoribbons in two- and three-terminal setups with proximitized sectors and asymptotic normal leads. Our focus is on the regime of single chiral Majoranas. The characteristic electric and thermal interferometries of chiral Majoranas can be controlled by the complex phases of the pairing. We predict an AC Majorana effect, in which phase dynamics induced by a voltage bias generate measurable time-dependent conductance oscillations. A three-terminal junction with superconducting islands can be used as a Majorana router when the relative complex phases are configured.
summary: This work theoretically analyzes charge and heat transport in magnetic topological insulator nanoribbons coupled to multiple superconductors. By controlling the relative superconducting phases, researchers predict unique interference effects, including an AC Majorana effect and the ability to build a phase-controlled 'Majorana router' device. This highlights superconductivity phase control as a powerful tool for manipulating topological quantum channels.
main_problem: The study investigates how superconducting phase differences control charge and heat transport through magnetic topological insulator nanoribbons containing multiple proximitized superconducting sectors.
main_result: The system exhibits phenomena like an AC Majorana effect (time-dependent conductance oscillations) and the ability to function as a tunable, phase-controlled Majorana router in three-terminal junctions.
method: The analysis employs analytical scattering matrix techniques combined with numerical diagonalization of the Hamiltonian across different superconducting/normal regions.
model_or_system: The physical system is an MTI nanoribbon structured into two- and three-terminal devices, where superconductivity is induced via proximity coupling ($\Delta_{p,m}(x)$). The transport is mediated by chiral Majorana modes.
key_observables: Electrical conductance ($G$), thermal conductance ($K$), and time-dependent conductance oscillations (AC effect).
important_parameters: Superconducting phase differences ($\phi_{12}, \phi_{13}, \phi_{23}$), separation lengths ($\ell$), and segment lengths ($L_s$).
main_assumptions: The analysis focuses on the regime mediated by a single chiral Majorana mode, and numerical methods are applied even for short superconducting segments.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematics of two-terminal (NSN/NSNSN) and three-terminal junctions. Plots show conductance ($G$) and thermal conductance ($K$) dependence on phase differences ($\phi_{12}$) and separation lengths ($\ell$), demonstrating blockade and interference effects.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the role of superconducting phases in MTI transport, deriving scattering relations for two-terminal junctions (NSN), analyzing charge mediation, and culminating in a detailed study of phase control in three-terminal 'Majorana router' configurations.
why_interesting: The explicit dependence on complex superconducting phases ($\phi$) to modulate quantum transport signatures like conductance blockade or AC oscillations provides a direct platform for engineering topological quantum states using external electromagnetic control (voltage bias).

The figure also indicates the transverse width of the supercon- ducting regions (Ly), as well as the lengths of the proximitized segments (LS) and their separation (ℓ).

Charge of the right-going mode that connects the two superconductor regions as a function of the phase accu- mulated L = kℓdue their separation and the phase difference ϕ12 ≡ϕ1 −ϕ2 between them. Note that the charge of this mode is independent of ξ and therefore is also independent of the superconductor length Ls.

FIG. 5. Results from numerical modeling. Upper panels show the probability density distributions ρ, while the lower panels display the charge density ρc. Panels (a) and (c) correspond to ℓ= 13.3 µm, whereas panels (b) and (d) correspond to ℓ= 4.4 µm. The remaining parameters are Ly = 2.5 µm, Ls = 20 µm, ϕ12 = π/2, α = 0.2 meV µm, m0 = 17 meV, and ℏm1 = 10−3 meV µm2. Additionally, ∆t = 1 meV and ∆b = 0 in the superconducting regions.
